title: Graumark was forged this morning from one line I typed. Campaign Forge, the 2D tactical Infinite Story RPG that forges a new world for every player, enters Early Access on November 27
author: DaedalusR8
selftext:
![img](s4v8n751sk2i1 "In-Game \"World Card\" generated with basic Information for a newly created world.")

Some of you have followed Campaign Forge here since the summer. It enters Steam Early Access on November 27, so here is the game the way you will play it.

You type a vision for a world (a single line is enough) and create a hero and a party. The game forges the world around them: regions, factions, a cast of people, and your companions woven into its history by name. Then it writes the campaign chapter by chapter around the choices you make, for as long as you want to play, and the world remembers: oaths, deaths and betrayals carry into the next chapter. Your words stay binding. The name your vision gives the world is its name, and every place it names is a real place in it.

The world in the picture came from one word: “Graumark”. I set what it is about to “A Secret to Uncover”, one of the kinds of world you can pick, next to A Foe to Face, Rival Powers and The Open Road (or you let your world-vision-prompt decide). In a secret world each chapter brings one trace to light, then the truth behind them all, and once the truth is out the world lives with it and you choose at camp what it is about next. That was what I wanted most from an endless campaign: a reason for the next chapter. The card itself is the game’s own, one click after any world is forged.

Gameplay-wise it's a tactical RPG with five ways to play: exploration, grid tactical combat, classic turn-based combat, directed cinematic scenes, and a branching visual novel. Grid fights run on a classic turn order with a real-time clock on top: the boss’s attacks count down in seconds, whoever’s turn it is. You STOP time to pull allies out and counter, SLOW it, FLATTEN a real-time attack back onto the turn order, or let it run. There are ten classes across six roles, your whole party fights, each member with their own gear and abilities, and when you want a break from the story, the Crucible has 60 hand-crafted boss floors in three boss-rush towers.

Everything the game makes is yours to change. Seventeen in-game tools let you paint maps, bring your own pictures in as sprites, design bosses and whole boss towers, forge boss abilities and sound effects, and author cutscenes, items, animations, battlefields that fight back and exploration events, and what you make, the game uses in the worlds it forges. Modding is a folder: drop a file in and it is in the game on the next launch, more than 50 kinds of content. All of it is generated on your own PC by the AI that ships with the game: offline, no account, no subscription.

The free demo has three acts. The Ember Road is a hand-made chapter that starts instantly (about 30 minutes, it's essentially a short no-AI Demo of the games overall mechanics). Forge a New Campaign builds your own world and its first two chapters (it's the actual generator), which takes a few minutes on a modern graphics card and longer on an older PC. Forge a Boss opens the boss designer and an arena to fight your creation in. Demo progress carries into the full game, where the tools unlock with points you earn by playing.



\----------------------

  
I don’t write the code. Campaign Forge is made by me with Claude (Anthropic) as lead developer: over 2,200 commits since March, none typed by me. I design, decide, review and play; Claude writes the code, the documentation, the test scripts and the first draft of every patch note.

Documentation is what holds that together across months. Claude keeps the project’s memory itself, close to 500 documents by now, one for each system, plan, decision or mistake, under an index it reads at the start of every session. Plans go into that memory before any code is written, and the docs change in the same piece of work as the code they describe. At the top of the index sit nearly 60 hard rules, many written the day something went wrong: read the log before answering a bug, measure instead of asking me to look, a one-way map-exit is a broken map-exit, more...

Debugging runs on my playtest rounds. I play a fresh world from start to finish and write up everything that’s off, screenshots included; each round becomes its own document, named after the world it happened in. Answers have to start from the game’s session log and the pixels in the screenshot, never from a theory. More than 240 headless probe scripts run parts of the game without a window and check that a rule still holds, often written in the same commit as the fix they protect, and before an upload the exported game is booted and its log read, since an export can behave differently from the editor. What Claude still gets wrong is judgment rather than syntax: fixing a symptom instead of its cause, or calling something done that nobody has played yet. That’s what the rules and the playtests are for.



Tl;dr what makes this project work is: \***Documentation**\*, debugging/logging and playtesting from both Claude and myself. Pretty much the same as any good Software was supposed to be made pre-AI aswell, so nothing new there.
